title: Four senses of fiducia — rest in God, grace-persuasion, fortitude, conscience-quiet
source_text: XCVI. Praecipue vero Scholae Reformatae Theologi de fiducia varie loquuntur: dum quidam dicunt, ut supra visum est, fiduciam esse partem fidei primariam, & proprium illius actum, alii vero istud negant, & docent fiduciam esse quidem fidei prolem atque effectum, sed non tamen actum ejus proprie dictum: ac praeterea fiduciae nomine, alii quidem istud, alii vero aliud intelligunt. Qua de re ut mentem nostram aperiamus, repetendae sunt variae fiduciae acceptiones, quae supra fuerunt a nobis recensitae. Primum ergo fiduciae nomine intelligitur actus ille per quem in Deum recumbimus, illi innitimur, & ei adhaeremus; tanquam fonti & authori salutis, ut vitam & salutem ab eo consequamur. Secundo, fiducia apud multos designat firmam persuasionem de gratia & venia a Deo impetrata, & de nostra cum eo reconciliatione. Tertio, fiducia sumitur pro spirituali fortitudine, & animositate, qua animi nervos & robur opponimus iis malis & periculis quibuscum in hac vita mortali confligimus. Denique, fiducia sumitur pro conscientiae serenitate & tranquillitate, seu pro spirituali quadam securitate, quae opponitur timori servili.
pass_a_gloss: But especially the Theologians of the Reformed School speak variously concerning trust: while some say, as has been seen above, that trust is the primary part of faith and its proper act, others deny that, and teach that trust is indeed the offspring and effect of faith, but not yet its act properly so called: and besides, by the name of trust some understand one thing, others another. That we may open our mind on this matter, the various acceptations of trust which were recounted by us above are to be repeated. First therefore by the name of trust is understood that act by which we recline upon God, lean upon him, and adhere to him; as to the fountain and author of salvation, that we may obtain life and salvation from him. Second, trust among many designates a firm persuasion of grace and pardon obtained from God, and of our reconciliation with him. Third, trust is taken for spiritual fortitude and courage, by which we oppose the nerves and strength of the mind to those evils and dangers with which we struggle in this mortal life. Finally, trust is taken for the serenity and tranquillity of conscience, or for a certain spiritual security, which is opposed to servile fear.
pass_b_english: Reformed speak variously of fiducia: some call it faith’s primary proper act; others only faith’s offspring/effect — and the name itself shifts.

Four acceptations Le Blanc repeats: (1) reclining on God as salvation’s fountain; (2) firm persuasion of obtained grace, pardon, and reconciliation; (3) spiritual fortitude against life’s evils; (4) conscience-quiet / spiritual security against servile fear.
